turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Err, before ye start, I've his bloods. The INR is three point eight. Pressure was one hundred and forty two over eighty four, pulse seventy six.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Three point eight. Mm. That's a shade over the 2 to 3 we like. Come on in and sit yourself down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Traffic was desperate. I'm grand though, hardly worth the trip. They only rang about the bloods.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll go through it anyway. You're on the warfarin for the atrial fibrillation, yes?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, five-ish years now. The five milligram tablet, once a day. Not a bother.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't let him skip the rest, doctor. He's on Mizartan as well, forty milligrams, for the pressure.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): And the Omprazole, twenty milligram in the morning, for a bit of heartburn. Sure that's nothing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Did someone start an antibiotic on you somewhere else?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Out of hours last week, for a cough. Clarithromycin, 500, twice a day, well actually twice a day, and two days left. Only a tickle, like.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was more than a tickle, he was barking at night. And just so it's not written on him, my mam, his wife, is on Metformine for her sugar.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't put her Metformine anywhere near his list. Umm. Any fever with all this?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Fever? No. Not a bit of one.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your weight shifted at all?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Same as ever.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the cough itself, is it still about?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Err. It's there and it isn't. Mostly gone. Nothing to be writing down.
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's gone off the cabbage and the spinach this last fortnight. Leaves them on the plate.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of wind, that's all. I just pushed them aside. It's grand.

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right so, let me think it out. Clarithromycin can lift the INR, and easing off the greens takes the vitamin K down, so the warfarin works harder. I'm not surprised we're at three point eight.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): It's only a number. I'm not bleeding.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bruising you've spotted, or blood in the urine, or black stools?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I keep telling ye I'm grand.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. Let me see your arms. No bruising there. And the chest sounds clear enough.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So my working impression is the INR is up from the antibiotic and the diet change, not from a bleed. Nothing surer than that until we repeat it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I knock the warfarin on the head then? Seems an awful fuss.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, don't stop it. I'd drop you from five milligrams down to four milligrams once a day, starting this evening.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will I put the cabbage back on the dinner?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the greens steady, a similar portion most days. Don't binge on them and don't cut them out. And finish the clarithromycin, there's only the two days.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Four milligrams. If you say so. Still think I'm fine.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll repeat the INR in a week, and I'll see you back here in a week the same day.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll have him here. He'll pretend he doesn't need to come.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): I'll come. I'm not that contrary.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the bloods for this day week, first thing.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. So that's four milligrams from tonight, INR in a week, and in to me after.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Sure look, a lot of talk over nothing.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get a big bruise or any bleeding, don't sit on it, ring the surgery. The visit in a week stands either way.

spec.situation: Older patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation; INR result read aloud; antibiotic started elsewhere; green leafy diet changes; dose adjusted and recheck in a week.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Atrial fibrillation and five-ish years supported; duration was reported by patient, not doctor.
